newsitem.title: KYRGYZSTAN: Kyrgyzstan aims to double GDP by 2005 -- Akayev.
newsitem.headline: Kyrgyzstan aims to double GDP by 2005 -- Akayev.

text.p: Kyrgyz President Askar Akayev on Tuesday said the economy had stabilised and the government aimed to double gross domestic product by 2005.

"Kyrgyzstan's economy has begun to stabilise and industry is showing signs of life," Akayev said in a two-hour address to parliament in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek, where he outlined the former Soviet republic's 1997 budget.
He forecast GDP growth for 1996 at five percent, the country's first growth since gaining independence in 1991. GDP fell by 6.2 percent last year.
Akayev said he aimed to increase GDP by 7.2 percent in 1997 and by 7.2 percent each succeeding year until 2005, by which time GDP should have doubled, he said.
Akayev predicted inflation for 1996 at no more than 27 percent, down from 32 percent last year. He said he aimed to rein in inflation further in 1997 to 15 percent.
He put the country's 1996 budget deficit at 6.2 percent of GDP, and said he planned to reduce it to 5.7 percent in 1997. Last year's budget deficit was 11.4 percent of GDP.
Akayev said a greater proportion of government spending would be financed by state treasury bills.
Akayev, a 51-year-old former physicist, trounced challengers from the republic's former Communist elite in elections last December.
But the transition to a market economy, backed by the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, has been tough.

This mountainous nation bordering China relies mainly on farming and gold, and most industry has ground to a halt. Plant left over from the communist era includes a torpedo factory and a refinery to process Cuban sugar.
